newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian stocks bolstered by Wall Street.
newsitem.headline: Asian stocks bolstered by Wall Street.

text.p: Stock markets across most of Asia leapt higher on Thursday, propelled by another record on Wall Street overnight.
"The market is taking its lead from the U.S.," said Julian Ings-Chambers, assistant director at BZW Securities Asia in Hong Kong. "And there is nothing negative on the horizon," he added.

The Dow Jones Industrial average's 103.52-point advance to 6,961.63 on Wednesday was sparked by a rally in technology shares on strong earnings from semiconductor equipment maker Applied Materials. Other sectors soon succumbed to the euphoria.
Tokyo stocks shot higher at the opening and the momentum was maintained by strong buying of blue chip stocks.
The key Nikkei 225 average rose 411.76 points, or 2.24 percent, to 18,821.72. It later dropped to around 18,700, or about 1.50 percent up from the opening.
"The weak yen is the only remedy left for the Japanese economy, and it has helped blue-chip issues," said Hiroyuki Nakai, chief investment strategist at Nikko Securities Co Ltd.
Traders said sentiment in Japan improved after an official of the Liberal Democratic Party said on Wednesday that public money could be used to protect certain bank creditors.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index slipped back from an early 120-point rise and was up 37.36 points, or 0.28 percent, in mid-afternoon on 13,499.97.
Lingering concerns about politics, the Hong Kong dollar, and the property market continue to overhang the market.
"On a 12-month view, I am still pretty positive on Hong Kong, although over the next month or two we expect a bit of consolidation," Morgan Stanley's regional strategist, Peter Churchouse said.
Meanwhile, the dollar's recent surge was capped by remarks by an official of the Bundesbank, Germany's powerful central bank, that mark weakness was a concern for the bank.

"It is our concern at the moment... that the markets are still in literal respect of the dollar...is the development we have to mention," Bundesbank vice-president Johann Wilhelm Gaddum said at a meeting in Bangkok.

South Korean stocks advanced as investors stepped up to buy on improved market sentiment. News that a high-ranking North Korean official had defected to the South had little impact, despite initial concerns about renewed tensions in the area.
Stocks were up 4.21 points, or 0.59 percent, at 716.71.
Expectations of a recovery in the semiconductor market bolstered chip makers, traders said. Samsung Electronics, the world's leading chip maker, rose 3,400 won to 59,700.
Taiwan shares closed at a six-year high, aided by Wall Street's gains. The weighted index closed 112.18 points, or 1.51 percent higher, at 7,536.28.
Thai shares, however, fell victim to heavy selling amid continued concerns over the baht's slide against the U.S. dollar. The SET Index was down 19.47 points, or 2.69 percent, at 703.10.
Philippine shares forfeited early Dow-inspired gains to end lower. The main index closed 4.10 points down, or 0.12 percent, at 3,335.73 points.
Jakarta shares continued higher after breaking a record on Wednesday, with blue chips leading the market. The Jakarta Composite Index was up 2.359 points, or 0.34 percent, at 703.414.
Singapore stocks also rallied, with the Straits Times Index up 30.04 points, or 1.35 percent, at 2254.68, while Malaysian shares were up 10.52 points, or 0.84 percent, 1,264.94.
